title: Dynamics 365 Business Central: AL transaction isolation levels and cache usage.
summary: Runtime version 11 added Record.ReadIsolation, which overrides a transaction's isolation level for reads on one record instance. The NST record cache only answers Get() calls under Default or ReadUncommitted. ReadCommitted, RepeatableRead and UpdLock send every Get() to SQL Server, which can slow repeated reads a lot. The author argues that RepeatableRead and UpdLock could safely use the cache once the lock is held.
key_points: Record.ReadIsolation sets the isolation level for reads on a specific record instance, overriding the transaction's table-level isolation
Business Central caches records in Global (shared per server instance) and Private (per user and company) caches; Query objects do not use this cache
Only Default and ReadUncommitted serve Get() from the NST cache; higher levels force a SQL round-trip on every read
A test reading one Customer record 1000 times showed much slower execution under the higher isolation levels, relevant for scenarios like posting large orders
On-premises, cache sync between server instances defaults to 30 seconds and can be changed with CacheSynchronizationPeriod in CustomSettings.config

quotes.text: The NST record cache only serves Get() calls from cache when ReadIsolation is set to Default or ReadUncommitted.
quotes.why_it_matters: This is the core insight explaining why higher isolation levels cause dramatic performance degradation, as they bypass caching entirely and force database round-trips.

quotes.text: Once the isolation level goes up, it stays that way for the whole transaction.
quotes.why_it_matters: This behavior lock-in is critical for developers to understand because it means a single elevated isolation operation affects all subsequent table reads in that transaction.

quotes.text: This can be a measurable performance problem in production BC projects, but only under specific, fairly common conditions.
quotes.why_it_matters: Highlights that isolation level performance impact is real and should be carefully reviewed in production code, especially for batch operations like order posting.
